tier_reason: First-party README table vs Python re (per-pattern ms, 142 KB file, 200 iters, ReleaseFast); no CPU model stated and the Python-side comparison script is not in the repo (src/bench.zig only times nanoregex), so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1.65x-2.8x faster than Python re on 6 of the 7 patterns in the README table (Python re is 1.5x faster on `fn [A-Za-z]+\(.*alloc`); the README text claims '8 of 8 head-to-head non-anchored patterns won', which contradicts its own 7-row table. Separately ~5000x faster than zig-regex 0.1.1 on a catastrophic-backtracking pattern (43 s -> 8 ms), and a zigrep --regex query went from 43 s to 0.43 s end-to-end after switching engines.
corrections.workload: Regex findAll over a 142 KB Zig source file, 200 iterations, ReleaseFast build; 7 patterns in the README table (pure literal, literal-prefix, `fn [A-Za-z]+\(.*alloc`, \d+, [a-z]+, alternation foo|bar|baz, IPv4-like) vs Python's re module; plus a catastrophic-backtracking pattern vs predecessor zig-regex 0.1.1.
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark: no CPU model, and only the nanoregex side of the harness (src/bench.zig) is published; the script that timed Python re and zig-regex is not in the repo. README says '8 of 8' patterns won but its table has 7 rows with 1 loss. The ~5000x figure is vs zig-regex 0.1.1 (niche predecessor, backtracking engine), not a named category baseline; the relevant comparison is 1.65x-2.8x vs Python re (widely used, not on the named-baseline list). Very small/new project (2 stars), kept per the DO-NOT-EXCLUDE-ON-SIZE rule.

notes: README numbers verified; record miscounted the table (said 7 of 8 wins, table shows 6 of 7) and the README's own '8 of 8' line is inconsistent. Metadata (MIT, 2 stars, last commit 2026-06-23, not fork/archived) matches gh.

tier_reason: README gives only first-party ranges vs RE2 (same speed / 20-30% / up to 100x) pointing at repo perf tests test/32-markdownish.cc and test/30-long.cc (make ... ENABLE_PERF_TESTS=1), with no timings, compiler, flags, or CPU; the >50x figure with unstated flags also caps it at C.

corrections.caveats: First-party README claim with no CPU model, compiler, flags, or absolute timings (only ranges plus 'run this make target yourself'; perf tests are test/30-long.cc and test/32-markdownish.cc). Abandoned since 2016-11-25 (tagged, not excluded). The author's README notes newer re2 versions 'significantly improved Unicode charclass performance', so the up-to-100x figure is likely stale against current RE2. x86-64 only, \b/\B unsupported, and the README closes with 'don't use this thing either way.'

tier_reason: Third-party Tantivy-team suite with public code (engines/iresearch-26.03.1 Makefile + serenedb `bench` CMake preset, clang-21/lld-21 via repo Dockerfile, Release build) re-run by Tantivy maintainer Pascal Seitz (commit c2b2850f, 2026-05-30) with CPU stated in README (AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D). The cited commit f4149454 alone would not be A: its README still described an older AWS Xeon 8488C/Rust 1.89 environment that did not produce those numbers.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Project README says 'up to 5x faster than Lucene and Tantivy'. In the suite's current results.json (iresearch-26.03.1 vs lucene-10.4.0 / tantivy-0.26, best of 10 runs, Ryzen 7 9800X3D), per-collector geometric-mean speedup vs Lucene is 0.99x (TOP_10), 1.20x (TOP_100), 1.41x (TOP_1000), 1.67x (TOP_100_COUNT), 1.25x (COUNT), and vs Tantivy 1.15x-1.28x; >=5x vs Lucene occurs on about 0.1% of queries (max 8.5x on the single term query 'the') (derived from page data). Lucene 10.4.0 with BP doc reordering is faster than IResearch on TOP_10/TOP_100 mean latency. In the cited commit f4149454 (vs lucene-10.3.0 / tantivy-0.25) the geo-mean speedup was 1.14x-1.84x vs Lucene and 1.33x-1.48x vs Tantivy (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: IResearch: clang/clang++ 21 with lld 21 (repo Dockerfile, llvm-toolchain-noble-21), cmake --preset bench = CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, static executables, jemalloc (serenedb CMakePresets.json), built in Docker per engines/iresearch-26.03.1/Makefile (PGO targets exist but are not the default compile target). Tantivy 0.26: Rust 1.96.0, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release, lto=true, opt-level=3. Lucene 10.4.0: OpenJDK 21.0.11, -XX:+UseParallelGC, jdk.incubator.vector.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Manjaro Linux, kernel 7.0.3-1-MANJARO (README environment for the current results.json, re-run 2026-05-30 by a Tantivy maintainer); the hardware for IResearch's own submission run (commit f4149454, 2026-03-24) is undocumented.
corrections.workload: Search Benchmark, the Game (quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game): English Wikipedia corpus, AOL-derived queries (962 per collector) run as term/intersection/union/phrase/negated/intersection_union queries under TOP_10 / TOP_100 / TOP_1000 / TOP_100_COUNT / COUNT collectors; single-threaded, best of 10 runs, warm page cache; vs Lucene 10.4.0 (plus Lucene -bp variant), Tantivy 0.26 and PISA 0.8.2.
corrections.caveats: The 'up to 5x' headline is a per-query maximum; typical per-collector geo-mean gains vs Lucene 10.4.0 are ~1.0x-1.7x, IResearch is slower than Lucene on TOP_10 intersection (mean 390 vs 241 us) and union (372 vs 309 us), and Lucene with BP reordering beats it on TOP_10/TOP_100 means, so SereneDB's 'outperforms Lucene across every query type' is not borne out by the committed results. Results were contributed by the SereneDB team (PR #82), approved/merged by fulmicoton and 'confirmed by @PSeitz', then re-run by the Tantivy maintainers. Originally iresearch-toolkit/iresearch (now archived, 188 stars), moved into serenedb/serenedb iresearch/ by the same maintainers; is_fork_of left null.

notes: benchmark_url moved from the SereneDB-authored commit f4149454 (undocumented hardware; README env at that commit was stale) to the suite repo, whose current results.json is from Tantivy-maintainer commit https://github.com/quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game/commit/c2b2850fdc6d0462afd5f8dce1388962b399ef6c on the documented 9800X3D. The '5x' figure is not on the commit page; it is IResearch's own README framing and is overstated as a headline, hence downgrade. License Apache-2.0, 831 stars, last commit 2026-09-25 confirmed via gh.

tier_reason: Public harness quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game (engines/tantivy-0.26/Makefile + Cargo.toml, engines/lucene-10.4.0/Makefile) states Rust 1.96.0 with -C target-cpu=native/LTO/opt-level=3, OpenJDK 21.0.11 JVM flags, and CPU AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, so A stands; but its committed results do not show the ~2x win the README states.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README FAQ says 'approximately 2x faster than Lucene', but the linked suite's current results.json (tantivy-0.26 vs lucene-10.4.0, best of 10 runs, Ryzen 7 9800X3D) shows per-collector geometric-mean speedups of 0.83x (TOP_10, Lucene faster), 1.02x (TOP_100), 1.14x (TOP_1000), 1.31x (TOP_100_COUNT), 1.08x (COUNT) (derived from page data). Tantivy is faster on phrase queries (mean 1.35x-1.58x on TOP_100/TOP_1000/TOP_100_COUNT/COUNT) and negated/term queries, while Lucene is ~2x-2.6x faster on TOP_10 intersection and union and COUNT union (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Tantivy 0.26: Rust 1.96.0, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release with [profile.release] lto=true, opt-level=3 (engines/tantivy-0.26). Lucene 10.4.0: OpenJDK 21.0.11, java -XX:+UseParallelGC --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector (engines/lucene-10.4.0/Makefile).
corrections.workload: Search Benchmark, the Game: English Wikipedia corpus, stemming disabled; AOL-derived queries (2+ terms, >=1 phrase hit, 962 per collector) run as term/intersection/union/phrase/negated/intersection_union queries under TOP_10 / TOP_100 / TOP_1000 / TOP_100_COUNT / COUNT collectors; single-threaded, best of 10 runs after warm-up (page cache + JIT); Tantivy 0.26 vs Lucene 10.4.0 (plus a Lucene BP-reordering variant).
corrections.caveats: The README's '~2x faster than Lucene' is not borne out by the suite's committed results since at least Sept 2025 (tantivy-0.25 vs lucene-10.3.0 geo-means 0.90x-1.33x) and in the current run Tantivy is slower on TOP_10 and roughly at parity on TOP_100; the win is concentrated in phrase, term, negated and count-heavy (TOP_100_COUNT) workloads, and Lucene with BP doc reordering is faster still on most collectors. The live dashboard tantivy-search.github.io/bench/ is JS-rendered; ratios here are computed from results.json. Benchmark is maintained by the Tantivy team.

notes: Real, notable entry, but the headline claim is stale/overstated against Lucene 10.x, so downgrade on the claim with tier A kept; the orchestrator may want to reframe it as 'faster on phrase/count workloads' or reconsider inclusion. tier_reason: First-party README table vs ripgrep and grep (openclaw, 9K files, warm cache) with no CPU, rustc version, or repeat count; benches/bench.rs is a Criterion suite on synthetic repos that times frg only and never runs ripgrep, so the table has no public harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 5.3x faster than ripgrep on a selective literal search (renderUsage: 10ms vs 53ms); faster than ripgrep on all 8 tested pattern types (1.06x-5.3x); grep took 1,553ms vs frg 10ms on the same literal (~155x, derived from page data); README claims 100% match-count parity with ripgrep. frg timings exclude a one-time index build (~20-23 s for 9K files).
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark only; no CPU model, rustc version, or repeat count. benches/bench.rs benchmarks frg indexed vs brute-force search on synthetic 1K/5K-file repos and does not invoke ripgrep, so the ripgrep comparison is not reproducible from the repo. Indexed search vs ripgrep's index-free scan is not like-for-like: frg needs a one-time index build (~20-23 s for 9K files) and index updates after file changes.

notes: README numbers match the record; the ~150x vs grep is a ratio, now marked derived. Last commit is 2026-03-24 (record had 2026-09-24), still 'active'; MIT, 16 stars, not fork/archived.
